M01.1:
Visited the neurology suite at Cascade Summit late in the afternoon, which turned out to be the quieter half of the day, and we spent nearly all of the time on teaching rather than on anything scientific. This prescriber is taking the PGY2 rotation block again this year and described the schedule as heavier than expected, with two residents rotating through the epilepsy service at once and a third joining in the spring.

Journal club has moved to the first Thursday of the month, and the plan is to let the residents choose the papers themselves for the first half of the year; the reasoning offered was that trainees read more carefully when the choice is their own. I was asked, politely, whether medical affairs teams ever sit in on those sessions. I explained that I could not select or supply articles for a teaching curriculum, and that anything we discuss would go through the usual scientific exchange process, which the attending accepted without pushing further.

No materials were requested and no clinical topics were raised today. We also spent a minute on the new resident lounge, which is apparently smaller than the old one. I offered to come back once the rotation settles and we agreed to aim for mid-November, with the office manager confirming a slot. Nothing further to log from this visit.

M02.1:
Short appt, ~20 min, squeezed between clinic blocks. Pt volume up and one NP out on leave, so sched backlog is running six to eight weeks. That came up first and set the tone.

Asked what the gaps look like right now in the DRE population. Called the adolescent transition group the single biggest unmet need — drug-resistant focal seizures at 15 or 16, and cenobamate out of reach until 18. Said the same conversation repeats with parents every few months, and that nothing about it has changed since last yaer.

No request to use XCOPRI outside the label and I did not go there. Logged as an observation only.

Rest was logistics. Two pts referred in from the community side still waiting on video EEG slots. Fellow is covering f/u calls while the NP is out. Asked me to keep future visits in the Monday afternon window.

No materials requested. No AE discussed. Will flag the adolescent comment internally and f/u next quarter, probably Jan. Next appt not set — will coordinate w/ the front desk.

Nothing else to report from this interaction.

Told the prescriber I would check what is available at label level and bring it, nothing beyond that. No off-label discussion. No AE reported.

F/u: send interaction section reference from the XCOPRI label, confirm new clinic day, next visit Feb. Note to self — bring a printed copy, netowrk drive is blocked in that building.

M05.1:
Visit on January 20 at 11:00, thirty minutes as scheduled, third interaction with this center since September 2025.

First half was telehealth logistics. The center moved to a hybrid model in October and now runs roughly 40 percent of routine follow-ups remotely. The attending estimated that about one in five of those still converts to an in-person visit, usually because a repeat EEG is needed. Two coordinators handle the virtual queue, and the stated bottleneck is not the technology but the consent step, which currently takes a separate call. Noted for context only.

Second half turned to the adolescent population. The epilepsy program here follows patients from age 12 upward and transitions them internally at 18, so both sides of that line sit in the same clinic. Requested a literature package on cenobamate in patients under 18, even early-phase or PK work. I confirmed that I would search what is publicly available and reply in writing, and stated plainly that I could not comment on use outside the approved adult indication. That was accepted without further discussion.

No adverse events were discussed and no claims were made on my side.

F/u: reply by January 27 with whatever published pediatric or PK material on CNB exists, or written confirmation that none is available. Next visit targeted for the week of March 9.

M07.1:
A longer visit than planned — forty minutes, most of it in the reading room between EEG reviews, and the conversation moved through several topics before settling on the adolescent population.

We began with documentation, since the center switched EHR templates in April and the seizure-frequency field now accepts only one entry per encounter, which the attending finds genuinely unhelpful for patients whose events come in clusters. The workaround has been to put the detail in free text, where nobody can query it afterwards.

On the clinical side, I asked how the referral mix has shifted since last year. Sees a steady trickle of drug-resistant teens and called the 18-plus label 'a waiting room with no exit' for them. There was no suggestion of prescribing outside the approved indication and I did not raise it; the point being made was about the gap itself, and about what to tell families in the interim, which I said I would pass along internally as an observation.

Also mentioned one adult patient reporting persistent dizziness after the last titration step, now being watched closely. I thanked the physician for raising it, explained that I would report the case through our safety process today rather than handle it in this note, and confirmed that pharmacovigilance may follow up directly for details.

Follow-ups: submit the safety report the same day, log the adolescent observation, and return in September when the fellows rotate.
